strengths: Addresses a more challenging and natural model where rewards depend directly on hidden states rather than only on beliefs, extending prior work on contextual bandits with latent state dynamics.
Provides high-probability regret bounds for a fully adaptive strategy that estimates HMM parameters online, unlike prior analyses that assume known HMM parameters.
Introduces a staged LinUCB approach with a carefully constructed filtration and uses HMM forgetting properties to handle complex dependencies between rewards and hidden states.
Offers a detailed comparison to the simplified model of Nelson et al. (2022) and shows how the belief-dependent model reduces to linear contextual bandits.
The theoretical analysis is non-trivial and contributes to understanding the interplay between HMM estimation and bandit regret.
weaknesses: The main theorem's rate T^{7/8} is suboptimal. A correct optimization of the derived bound yields T^{5/6} with the same algorithm (e.g., choosing λ=ℓ=T^{2/3}). The paper's optimization step contains an error (using T^{3/2}/ℓ instead of T/√ℓ), leading to a suboptimal choice of parameters and a weaker result.

The belief estimation subroutine is only justified for finite context sets under restrictive Assumption 4.2 (full-rank emission matrix, positive minimum elements, stationary initial distribution). The general continuous context case is mentioned but not formally proven, leaving a gap in the main theorem's applicability.

The algorithm is computationally expensive: it re-estimates HMM parameters from scratch at each round using the spectral method, resulting in at least O(T^2) complexity. No computational considerations or practical implementation details are discussed.
No numerical simulations are provided; the paper explicitly states they will appear in a future version. This prevents verification of practical performance and reduces reproducibility.

Presentation is poor: numerous typos (e.g., 'partiel', 'Marhov', 'self-completedness'), inconsistent notation (\bm vs \pmb, \intercal vs \dagger vs \text{T}), and formatting issues (headers embedded in the middle of pages). The proofs are dense and hard to follow.

The high-probability bound relies on Markov's inequality, yielding a polynomial dependence on 1/δ rather than the logarithmic dependence typical of martingale-based bounds. This is a weaker form of high-probability guarantee.
The regret benchmark is a pseudo-regret against a belief-based oracle, not the true optimal policy that knows the hidden state. The paper acknowledges this but it limits the strength of the result.
The regret bound depends on an unknown constant T_{B,M,ν} that can be large depending on the HMM parameters, so the bound is not uniform over the HMM class and may be loose in practice.

strengths: Meaningful model extension: the paper studies rewards that depend directly on the hidden state (Eq. 1), which is genuinely more general than the belief-dependent reward model of Nelson et al. (2022). The authors give a plausible argument that the belief substitution is a real simplification, and they show the belief-dependent case reduces to a linear contextual bandit while the direct-state case does not.

The analysis targets high-probability regret bounds rather than bounds in expectation, and explicitly accounts for online estimation of HMM parameters, which prior analysis ignored. This is a legitimate strengthening of the guarantee type.

The staged LinUCB strategy and the carefully constructed intermediate filtration U_t (which is U_t-measurable for actions yet close to the context-only belief b_t via HMM forgetting) is a non-trivial and reasonably novel technical device.

The regret bounds are essentially 'reward-model free' apart from HMM-estimation terms (no dependence on reward gaps or population-design coverage), which is a real improvement over the constants appearing in Nelson et al.
Section 6 gives an honest limitations discussion, identifying that the T^{7/8} rate may be improvable and pinpointing the L^2-Markov argument (1/sqrt(delta) dependence) as the source of the loss.
weaknesses: No empirical validation whatsoever. Appendix F is a placeholder ('Numerical simulations will be provided in a version 2 of this article'), yet Appendix C.4 refers to 'our numerical experiments,' indicating the paper is incomplete and internally inconsistent. For a paper that also claims a 'more efficient treatment,' the absence of any practical evidence is a serious deficiency.

Suboptimal and poorly motivated rates: T^{7/8} for the general model is worse than the T^{3/4} of the simplified model, and the authors themselves concede it may be improvable to T^{3/4}. No lower bounds are provided to establish whether T^{7/8} or even T^{3/4} is near-optimal, so the significance of the main result is unclear.

The results rest on a stack of strong assumptions: Assumption 4.1 (a fully known belief-error function with sum_t U_belief(t,delta) = O~(T^{1/2})), Assumption 4.2 (finite context set, full-rank emission matrix, invertible transition with strictly positive entries), and Assumption 5.1 (exponentially fast forgetting). The general theorem needs all of them simultaneously, sharply limiting the scope of the contribution.

Presentation quality is poor and contains correctness-relevant errors: many typos ('partiel', 'Manhov chain', 'squar', 'self-completedness'), a corrupted transpose symbol in Eq. (5), and broken/incorrect cross-references — Nelson et al. is reference [19] but is repeatedly cited as '[20]' (e.g., the 'Comparison to [20] ([2022])' heading), and the related-work discussion conflates reference numbers. These make the paper difficult to verify and read.

The head-to-head comparison with Nelson et al. is not apples-to-apples: the paper contrasts its high-probability T^{3/4} bound against Nelson et al.'s expected sqrt(T) bound, and asserts the T^{1/4} gap is 'only' due to belief estimation without rigorously establishing that claim. The core comparative advantage is therefore asserted rather than proven.

The central modeling claim — that direct hidden-state dependence is 'the more natural model' — is subjective and not strongly justified. The belief-dependent model is also a legitimate (and arguably more learnable) formulation, so the framing overstates the importance of the extension.

The algorithm requires the horizon T to be known in advance (used to set lambda = ell = T^{3/4}), and relies on a belief-estimation subroutine whose constants (e.g., Delta' in Anandkumar et al.) are not available in closed form, complicating practical instantiation and reproducibility.

strengths: The paper studies a more natural and challenging model than prior work: rewards depend directly on unobserved HMM states, contexts, and actions, while contexts and rewards are governed by latent dynamics. It provides the first sublinear high-probability regret bound for this setting, which is a meaningful theoretical advance.

It gives a simpler and more direct analysis of the simplified belief-dependent model of Nelson et al. (2022), obtaining a high-probability T^{3/4} bound while explicitly accounting for belief-estimation error. This improves on prior expected-only bounds that ignored HMM parameter estimation.

The staged LinUCB strategy on estimated beliefs is technically well motivated. The construction of the filtration U_t to balance action measurability and closeness between conditional beliefs is a neat idea, and the use of HMM forgetting properties is carefully integrated into the analysis.

The paper extends the elliptic potential lemma to staged updates and adapts an L^2-Markov argument to control non-martingale terms. These are nontrivial technical contributions that may be useful beyond the specific setting.

The limitations are discussed honestly, including the suboptimal T^{7/8} rate, the open question of whether T^{3/4} is achievable in the general model, and the role of the L^2-Markov argument in worsening the dependence on the failure probability.
weaknesses: The presentation is below the standard expected for ICML. There are numerous typos (e.g., 'partiel', 'Marhov', 'defintion'), inconsistent notation (e.g., \tilde{b} vs. \widehat{b}), repeated sections (Assumption 4.1 and Lemma 4.3 appear twice), and mislabeled assumptions (Assumption 2.3 is a bounded second-moment condition, not sub-Gaussian, yet is referred to as sub-Gaussian in Theorem 5.2). These issues make the paper unnecessarily hard to follow.

No numerical simulations are provided; Appendix F states they will appear in a 'version 2'. For a paper that proposes a new algorithm and claims practical relevance, the absence of any empirical validation is a significant weakness. It also leaves unclear how the algorithm behaves computationally and statistically in practice.

The belief-estimation subroutine is abstract and only instantiated under quite strong assumptions: finite context set, full-rank emission matrix, positive minimum entries in the emission and transition matrices, invertible transition matrix, and stationary initial distribution. Moreover, the spectral method is recomputed at every round, which is computationally expensive; the paper does not discuss how to make the procedure online or efficient.

The main regret rate T^{7/8} is suboptimal and very close to linear. No lower bounds are given to assess whether this rate is near-optimal or whether the gap to T^{3/4} is fundamental. The paper suggests T^{3/4} might be achievable but does not prove it.

The comparison to Nelson et al. (2022) is not entirely apples-to-apples: the simplified-model analysis assumes sub-Gaussian noise (Assumption 2.2), whereas Nelson et al. use a milder bounded second-moment condition (Assumption 2.3). The paper argues this relaxation is unimportant, but this is a subjective judgment, and the claimed 'stronger' bound partly relies on a stronger noise assumption.

The regret benchmark is a pseudo-regret defined with respect to beliefs based only on contexts, not on the full observed history including past rewards. This is a weaker benchmark than one using all observed information, and the algorithm deliberately ignores reward information for state inference. Although the authors argue this benchmark is intrinsic, it limits the strength of the guarantees.

The claim that the bounds do not depend on the reward functions is overstated: the bounds depend on C_{\theta^*} and C_\eta, which are reward/noise-related constants, as well as on HMM parameters such as \gamma. The intended meaning (no dependence on reward gaps) is reasonable, but the wording is imprecise.

The algorithm requires knowledge of the horizon T to set \lambda and \ell, and the regret bound depends on the unknown threshold T_{\mathcal{B},M,\nu} of the belief-estimation subroutine. While these are common in theoretical bandit work, the paper does not discuss practical tuning or the impact of misspecifying T.
